title: On‑prem control plane proxy queue backpressure — incident review and runbook draft
content:
Summary:

During a mid-day traffic surge on 2026-04-10 we observed broad control plane lag for on-prem customers using the lightweight control‑plane proxy (v2.3.1). The proxy's internal request queue reached built-in soft limits and began queuing client requests for config fetches and heartbeat traffic; as a result control plane heartbeats were delayed up to 90s for some nodes and several customers reported transient 'control plane unreachable' symptoms.

Impact:
- Several on-prem clusters (4 customers) experienced delayed control-plane operations: configuration sync lag, transient agent reconnections, and delayed rollout progress.
- No data loss, but customer-managed controllers reported degraded health checks and automation retries.
- Incident window: ~2026-04-10 14:12 — 2026-04-10 15:00 UTC (mitigation applied 14:29 UTC, stabilization by 14:58).

How it was detected:
- Alert: increase in controlplane.request_queued_count per-proxy (threshold 200) from 14:10 UTC.
- Pager duty triggered for oncall eng-private-deployments.
- Slack #oncall-private thread created, logs linked in linked_artifacts.

Timeline (abridged):
- 14:08 UTC: rolling customer traffic increase begins (scheduled batch jobs + customer spike).
- 14:10 UTC: controlplane.request_queued_count crosses alert threshold on 3 proxies.
- 14:12 UTC: oncall identifies high queue depth and growing per-request latency; initial hypothesis: downstream control-plane DB slow.
- 14:15 UTC: tcpdump from proxy to controlplane shows many TCP connections in ESTABLISHED but no progress (requests stuck in proxy send queue).
- 14:20 UTC: additional metrics show many long-lived idle backend connections owned by proxy; some customer firewalls are known to drop idle connections after 60s without RST.
- 14:24 UTC: emergency mitigation: bumped proxy local request worker pool from 32 -> 64 and enabled aggressive connect fallback (open new connections instead of waiting).
- 14:29 UTC: queued depth starts decreasing; client latencies recover.
- 14:58 UTC: system considered stable; follow-up actions logged.

Immediate root cause hypothesis (short):
A combination of: (1) proxy connection reuse combined with insufficient TCP-level liveness probes, (2) customer-managed stateful firewalls silently dropping idle connections, and (3) a recent config change (candidate rollback) that reduced the default connection pool and removed a fallback path that previously opened new connections when requests stalled. The net effect: the proxy held many requests onto connections that were nominally ESTABLISHED but effectively dead; requests piled into an in-memory queue until the worker/queue soft limit was hit and new requests began to be queued or dropped.

Why this didn't trigger earlier:
- The proxy relied on TCP keepalive settings tuned for cloud regions (longer timeouts). Customer firewalls had shorter idle timeouts and did not send RSTs, causing silent blackholed connections.
- Our monitoring tracked socket counts but not queue age distribution per request path; older requests were hidden in aggregated latency percentiles.

Temporary mitigations performed during incident:
1) Increase local proxy worker pool (32 -> 64) and reduce per-request queue timeout to 10s (from 30s) to pressure fail-fast behavior.
2) Enabled 'connect-on-fail' fallback so the proxy will attempt a new connection when in-flight requests exceed a latency threshold.
3) Pushed a temporary control-plane routing policy to prefer regional endpoints with lower observed RTT for affected customers.
4) Notified the four affected customers with suggested firewall rules (allow persistent connections between proxy <-> controlplane, increase idle timeout to > 120s or enable TCP keepalive on firewall).

Concrete evidence & logs:
- tcpdump snippets showed data plane: many SYN/ACK flows with no application-layer bytes for 65+ seconds prior to request timeout.
- proxy logs: repeated 'request waiting on socket' messages and 'socket write returned EPIPE' for a subset of flows just after mitigation.
- metrics: controlplane.request_queued_count peaked at 512 for one proxy instance.

Detailed root cause analysis (long):
- Code/config change: 2026-04-01 config change reduced the default connection pool size from 64 -> 32 to reduce memory footprint (PR ref DP-1942). This reduced headroom during spikes.
- Proxy behavior: when a connection is reused, the proxy did not validate application-level heartbeat before writing; if the remote silently dropped the TCP state, writes could block or stall waiting for kernel retransmits. The proxy would then enqueue further user requests on that connection rather than opening a fresh connection immediately.
- Network behavior: several customer firewalls (edge appliances) implement idle TCP timeout ~60s and silently drop state without sending RSTs. Concurrently, NAT entries timed out earlier than backend keepalive. This mismatch caused backend destiny to be ESTABLISHED from proxy's TCP stack perspective but the path was effectively one-way.

Longer-term fixes (planned):
- Code-level: implement application-level pings (in-proxy heartbeat) before reusing idle connections and detect half-open connections faster. Add configurable probe interval per-deployment.
- Code-level: implement per-connection request queue limit and a circuit-breaker that opens new connections when queue age > X.
- Config/policy: restore connection pool to a safer default (64) and make default tied to observed QPS/len.
- Observability: add metric controlplane.request_queue_age_p50/p95/p99, and socket_stall_count per-proxy. Add synthetic probes that validate forward+return data path.
- Operations: build a customer-facing guidance doc for firewall/NAT settings for on-prem installs; add an item in onboarding checklist.
- Runbook: add explicit steps for diagnosing silent TCP drops (tcpdump flags, expected timestamps, socketstat queries).

Runbook draft — immediate playbook for oncall (short):
1) When controlplane.request_queued_count alert fires, immediately run: kubectl -n redwood proxy get pods -l app=control-proxy -o wide and identify top 3 pods by queued_count.
2) Capture live proxy metrics: curl http://localhost:6060/metrics | grep request_queued_count and request_queue_age; if request_queue_age_p95 > 10s, escalate.
3) Collect tcpdump on the proxy host for the controlplane upstream IP/port for 60s: sudo tcpdump -i eth0 host <controlplane-ip> and port <port> -w /tmp/proxy-conn.pcap
4) Check kernel socket backlog and retransmit counters: ss -tin state established | grep <controlplane-ip> and cat /proc/net/netstat (or use netstat -s) to inspect retransmits.
5) If many sockets appear ESTABLISHED with no bytes in the last 60s: execute mitigation (a) increase worker pool via rolling config (b) enable connect-on-fail fallback flag (yaml patch examples below).
6) Notify affected customers and coordinate firewall/NAT idle timeout adjustments (ask for > 120s or enable keepalive).

Runbook draft — config snippets (example):
- kube patch to increase worker pool: kubectl -n redwood patch deployment control-proxy --type='json' -p='[{"op":"replace","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/env/WORKER_POOL_SIZE","value":"64"}]'
- feature flag for connect-on-fail: set via configmap redwood-proxy-config: CONNECT_ON_FAIL=true

Post-incident action items (owners & ETA):
- A. Implement application-level probe and connection validation in proxy (PR opened) — owner: Marcus Patel — ETA: 2026-04-30 — JIRA: DP-2010.
- B. Restore safer default connection pool and add auto-scaling logic — owner: Priya Das — ETA: 2026-04-22 — JIRA: DP-2011.
- C. Observability: add queue-age metrics and synthetic probe dashboards — owner: Sofia Rivera — ETA: 2026-04-20 — JIRA: DP-2012.
- D. Customer onboarding doc for firewall/NAT requirements — owner: Avery Chen — ETA: 2026-04-21 — Confluence draft linked in linked_artifacts.

Notes to oncall and follow-up communications:
- When engaging with customers, request (1) firewall idle timeout, (2) NAT mapping timeout, (3) appliance vendor and firmware — sometimes firmware has aggressive idle cleanup bugs.
- Prioritize rolling out the connect-on-fail fallback as a short-term safe default for all on-prem deployments.
- Consider a small dark-launch of queue-age metrics in staging to validate alert thresholds.

Appendix — quick troubleshooting checklist (copyable):
- Identify affected proxies: curl metrics -> sort by request_queued_count
- Check queued age: request_queue_age_p95 > 10s => high risk
- tcpdump 60s on proxy -> inspect timestamps and payloads
- ss -tin for retransmits, netstat -s for TCP retransmit counters
- If confirmed: increase worker pool + enable connect-on-fail; notify customers; open incident ticket DP-INC-4123

This document is a working draft — please add logs, packet captures, and any customer correlating evidence to the linked_artifacts. After code fixes land, we should convert the runbook into the canonical SRE runbook page and schedule a short postmortem review with the affected customers and solutions engineering.

Owners for this doc: Avery Chen (author), with engineering review by Marcus Patel and Priya Das.
